claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
The baseline alloy has a density of approximately 12-13 g/cm³.
The baseline alloy has a room-temperature yield strength of approximately 830 MPa.
The baseline alloy has less than 5% room-temperature elongation.
Adding 2-4 at.% Al will produce a 5-10% volume fraction of ordered B2/NiAl-type precipitates in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The B2 precipitates will self-assemble into a reticulated or basketweave-like network within the BCC matrix.
The proposed B2 precipitates will be nanoscale and coherent or semi-coherent with the BCC matrix.
Homogenization annealing at 1200-1300°C for 24 hours will promote precipitation of the ordered B2 phase.
The reticulated intermetallic network will deflect and blunt cracks by forcing them onto tortuous propagation paths.
Crack deflection by the reticulated network will increase fracture toughness and room-temperature ductility.
The ordered precipitates will increase yield strength through Orowan strengthening.
The intervention will increase yield strength by 15-25%, to approximately 950-1050 MPa.
The intervention will increase uniform elongation from less than 5% to 15-25%.
The modified alloy will have a density of approximately 12.2-12.5 g/cm³, representing an increase of less than 2%.
Keeping Al below 5 at.% will avoid excessive embrittlement or formation of a continuous brittle network.
Cooling rate and homogenization time will control the volume fraction and morphology of the B2 precipitates.
A 3 at.% Al alloy quenched from 1200°C will contain no B2 precipitates and will exhibit only solid-solution hardening.
Similar ductility improvements in quenched and precipitation-annealed samples would favor solid-solution hardening over the proposed phase-structure mechanism.
Crack-deflection patterns observed by SEM would be unique to the reticulated precipitate network.

contradictions.description: The baseline density is given as 12-13 g/cm³, while the modified density is 12.2-12.5 g/cm³ and is described as an increase. These ranges do not consistently imply an increase; relative to portions of the stated baseline range, the predicted value would instead be a decrease.

The operating regime is uniaxial compression, but the ductility outcomes are expressed as elongation and uniform elongation, which are tensile metrics and are not directly produced by the specified compression test.
